name: Nebraska Territory government
sources: STAT 10 Stat. 277 secs 2 and 12; NOTE-governments-stores-1861 s.2
notes: An organised territory: a governor appointed by the President with the Senate's consent, removable by him (Act of 30 May 1854). Faction union is the model's reading that a territorial government is the federal government's own creature [design parameter, note s.2.3]. The act (sec. 1) keeps treaty Indian lands outside the Territory until the tribe assents, and Native nations held or claimed much of the land. This is the Territory's government, not the government of the nations who lived there.

name: Dakota Territory government
sources: STAT 12 Stat. 239 secs 2 3 11; NOTE-governments-stores-1861 s.2
notes: Organised by the Act of 2 March 1861, three days before the start; no governor in place until Jayne (nominated 23 March 1861, in Yankton by May-June). Faction union as for tr_nebraska [design parameter]. The act (sec. 1) excepts treaty Indian lands from the Territory until the tribe assents, and Native nations held or claimed much of the land. This is the Territory's government, not the government of the nations who lived there.

name: Colorado Territory government
sources: STAT 12 Stat. 172 secs 2 3 11; KAPPLER 12 Stat. 1163; NOTE-governments-stores-1861 s.2
notes: Organised by the Act of 28 February 1861; Gilpin was appointed after 4 March and reached Denver on 29 May 1861 (one source says 21 May). Faction union as for tr_nebraska [design parameter]. The act (sec. 1) excepts treaty Indian lands from the Territory until the tribe assents, and Native nations held or claimed much of the land. The treaty of Fort Wise, a cession signed by Cheyenne and Arapaho chiefs on 18 February 1861, was not yet ratified on 5 March (ratified 6 August 1861; KAPPLER, 12 Stat. 1163). This is the Territory's government, not the government of the nations who lived there.

name: New Mexico Territory government
sources: STAT 9 Stat. 446 secs 3 and 12; NOTE-governments-stores-1861 s.2
notes: Organised by the Act of 9 September 1850; the pack's arizona region lay inside it until the Arizona act of 24 February 1863 (secondary source). Governor on 5 March 1861: Abraham Rencher, Buchanan's appointee (secondary source). Faction union as for tr_nebraska [design parameter]; the territory's divided sympathies are for situations. The clauses of the 1850 act read here carry no exception for treaty Indian lands, but Native nations lived on and held or claimed much of the land [needs-source]. This is the Territory's government, not the government of the nations who lived there.

name: District of Columbia government
sources: USCONST art. I sec. 8 cl. 17; STAT 2 Stat. 103 (Act of 27 February 1801); NOTE-governments-stores-1861 s.2
notes: Governed under Congress's exclusive legislation; the city corporations and the county's Levy Court (justices appointed by the President) sat beneath it. Faction union is a design parameter: the seat of the federal government.

name: Cherokee Nation government
sources: CSA-STAT treaty with the Cherokees, 7 October 1861; OR I-13 p.490; NOTE-indian-territory-1861-sources s.1
notes: Principal Chief John Ross, Assistant Principal Chief Joseph Verner and the Executive Council (James Brown, John Drew, William P. Ross); seat of government Tahlequah. On 5 March 1861 the nation had declared nothing: Ross proclaimed 'strict neutrality' on 17 May at Park Hill (OR I-13 p.490), and a General Convention of the Cherokee People at Tahlequah on 21 August authorised the treaty with the Confederacy of 7 October, made at Tahlequah. In Bahos's phrase (an outside historian's, to be used only as attributed) 'the pro-Union sentiment of the Cherokee full-bloods' slowed the Confederate regiment's raising; this note names no side for the whole nation.

name: Muscogee (Creek) Nation government
sources: CSA-STAT treaty with the Creek Nation, 10 July 1861; NOTE-indian-territory-1861-sources s.1
notes: Principal Chief Motey Kinnaird, and Icho Hacho, First Chief of the Upper Creeks; a General Council and a Council Ground (the treaty was ratified there on 20 July 1861). The nation was divided in 1861: the General Council's committee of seventeen signed the treaty with the Confederacy on 10 July, while Opothleyahola and the Muscogees 'remaining loyal to Opothleyahola' fled in winter 'to a neutral country' (James Scott); in Wallace Cook's words the war 'was just like a civil war between the Indians of the Creek Nation' (the Muscogee Nation's own study guide, oral histories of the 1930s). One department; this note must not read as unanimity.

name: Seminole Nation government
sources: CSA-STAT treaty with the Seminole Nation, 1 August 1861; NOTE-indian-territory-1861-sources s.1
notes: Principal Chief John Jumper (Hin-i-ha Micco), twelve town chiefs and a Council House. The treaty with the Confederacy was made at the Seminole Council House on 1 August 1861 and signed at the Seminole agency on 2 August; John Chupco is not among its signers. The Seminole Nation Museum (a museum of the Nation, not its government) says 'one-third of the Seminole people chose to remain with the Union', led by Big John Chupco, and moved to Kansas.

name: Choctaw Nation government
sources: OR I-1 p.682; OR I-3 p.594; CSA-STAT treaty with the Choctaws and Chickasaws, 12 July 1861; KAPPLER treaty with the Choctaw and Chickasaw, 22 June 1855; NOTE-indian-territory-1861-sources s.1
notes: Principal Chief George Hudson (the Nation's own list of chiefs gives 1860-62; his proclamation of 14 June 1861 at Doaksville is signed 'Principal Chief Choctaw Nation', OR I-3 p.594) and a General Council. The General Council's five resolutions of 7 February 1861 were conditional (OR I-1 p.682). The commissioners for the treaty of 12 July were 'appointed by the Principal Chief ... in pursuance of an act of the Legislature'. Hudson's election date is not sourced.

name: Chickasaw Nation government
sources: CSA-STAT treaty with the Choctaws and Chickasaws, 12 July 1861; KAPPLER treaty with the Choctaw and Chickasaw, 22 June 1855; NOTE-indian-territory-1861-sources s.1
notes: Governor Cyrus Harris [inferred: the Nation's own Hall of Fame page gives his terms as 1856-58 and 1860-62 but does not say he held office on 5 March 1861], a Legislature of House and Senate, capital Tishomingo; separate from the Choctaw Nation again by the treaty of 22 June 1855. The Governor approved resolutions of secession or independence on 25 May 1861 (the Nation's own pages differ in the word), and the Legislature elected the Chickasaw commissioners for the treaty of 12 July (treaty text): the Legislature acted and the Governor approved [I]. Emory's 'unworthy conduct of the governor of the Chickasaw Nation' (OR I-1 p.648) is his attributed view, never the narrator's.

name: Restored Government of Virginia
sources: WHEELING-ORDINANCES-1861 pp6-7; LEWIS-HWVM pp79-80; OR I-2 pp723-724
notes: Inactive until the 19 June reorganisation notice is approved and loaded; no side until recognition through department_side. [I] Eight whole pack regions intersect the 35 counties on the completed credentials roll (Lewis pp79-80). This is an administrative approximation, neither a sovereignty boundary nor military control. The roll splits parkersburg, kanawha, wv_central and potomac_highlands; their extra counties are disclosed in notes/lane-1.11-situations.md. Moore represented Webster and parts of Nicholas and Braxton (Lewis p80 note), not those entire counties. The ordinance claims Virginia, not a new state.
